newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Milk scare not seen denting Nutricia.
newsitem.headline: Milk scare not seen denting Nutricia.

text.p: The withdrawal of Nutricia's Milumil baby milk powder in Britain following a scare over a possible link with salmonella was unlikely to have much impact on the Dutch specialist food giant, analysts said on Friday.

"The impact will be more severe for the Milumil brand name than for the company's financial performance," John David Roeg of Bank Labouchere said. "It will have almost no effect on Nutricia's profits."

Annual sales of the Milumil brand, produced exclusively for the British and Irish markets, were a very small part of its total milk formula sales, said ING analyst Gerard Rijk, and the company in any case carried ample provisions for such events.
Nutricia has around 11 million guilders ($6 million) set aside for dealing with contamination scares and the cost of the withdrawal might be only around one million guilders, he said.
Britain's Department of Health on Friday advised shopowners and consumers to stop selling and using the powdered milk formula, produced by Nutricia unit Milupa.

Nutricia said it had withdrawn the product as a precaution and stressed tests in the factory producing Milumil had shown no signs of salmonella. "We understand the Department of Health has not tested any of our products," it said in a statement.

Nutricia shares were suspended on the Amsterdam stock exchange after dropping 16.20 guilders on news of the recall, but pared some of the loss after they resumed trading to close down 9.70 guilders at 267.00.

Investors in the company were particularly sensitive to any scares of this type, Labouchere's Roeg said, meaning initial reactions were often overdone. The shares are still trading above their closing level at the end of last week.
Product volumes to be recalled were low, Roeg said, and the company would not be destroying these yet, also limiting the cost of the exercise.

The move by the British health authorities appeared to be very premature, ING's Rijk said, and Nutricia might even be able to recover its costs by means of legal action if no clear link to salmonella is subsequently identified.

"There is no conclusive proof," Nutricia said in its statement. "Although understandable, considering recent events in the UK, it is our feeling that the British health authorities have been overreacting."
Nutricia acquired Milupa in August 1995, increasing its group sales by over 65 percent and building a dominant over-forty-percent European infant milk formula market share.

The acquisition was integrated far faster than expected, with Nutricia posting a staggering 51 percent rise in first-half net profit in 1996 to 107.1 million guilders, attributed largely to the successful takeover.
However its core markets, infant milk formula, baby meals and cereals and clinical nutrition, make it particularly vulnerable to contamination scares.
"It will happen again," Roeg said. "Often it will be much ado about nothing, but that is the nature of the business."
"There's no real cause for alarm on Nutricia from this," he said. ($ = 1.835 Dutch Guilders)
